definition: Pattern theory, formulated by Ulf Grenander, is a mathematical formalism to describe knowledge of the world as patterns.
details: It differs from other approaches to artificial intelligence in that it does not begin by prescribing algorithms and machinery to recognize and classify patterns; rather, it prescribes a vocabulary to articulate and recast the pattern concepts in precise language. Broad in its mathematical coverage, Pattern Theory spans algebra and statistics, as well as local topological and global entropic properties. In addition to the new algebraic vocabulary, its statistical approach is novel in its aim to: Identify the hidden variables of a data set using real world data rather than artificial stimuli, which was previously commonplace. Formulate prior distributions for hidden variables and models for the observed variables that form the vertices of a Gibbs-like graph. Study the randomness and variability of these graphs. Create the basic classes of stochastic models applied by listing the deformations of the patterns. Synthesize (sample) from the models, not just analyze signals with them. The Brown University Pattern Theory Group was formed in 1972 by Ulf Grenander. Many mathematicians are currently working in this group, noteworthy among them being the Fields Medalist David Mumford. Mumford regards Grenander as his "guru" in Pattern Theory.

explainer.lead: Ulf Grenander's mathematical formalism for describing knowledge of the world as patterns. Rather than prescribing recognition algorithms, it supplies a vocabulary to express pattern concepts in precise language.

tiers.eli5: It is like agreeing on a careful set of words and rules for describing shapes and regularities before anyone builds a machine to spot them.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers use it as a conceptual and mathematical framework to formalize pattern problems across algebra, statistics and topology. Its breadth makes it hard to turn directly into an off-the-shelf algorithm.

explainer.example: Describing a class of objects through generators and transformations combined under statistical rules, so that observed instances can be expressed in the same vocabulary.
